The Mikhlol of the Generations: The Grammatical, Exegetical and Philosophical Teaching of Rabbi David Kimchi (Radak) in the Mirror of Culture and History
The text surveys the monumental work of Rabbi David Kimchi (Radak), a key figure who served as a cultural bridge between the tradition of Muslim Spain and the Jewry of Christian Europe in the Middle Ages. His principal works, chief among them the Sefer ha-Mikhlol, brought about a revolution in Hebrew linguistics by making accessible the method of the triliteral root and by fixing the division of the vowels that is accepted to this day. As a biblical commentator, Radak adhered to the rationalist approach of peshat (the plain sense), combining philological depth with philosophical thought and a polemical defense of Judaism in the face of Christianity. His decisive influence extended beyond the Jewish world, as his writings became the scholarly foundation for Christian scholars in the Renaissance and contributed to shaping the Western translations of the Bible.
The Mikhlol of the Generations: The Grammatical, Exegetical and Philosophical Teaching of Rabbi David Kimchi (Radak) in the Mirror of Culture and History
The figure of Rabbi David Kimchi (Radak), who was active in Narbonne in Provence between the years 4906 and 4995 (1160–1235), constitutes one of the most decisive and influential junctures in the history of Torah literature and Hebrew linguistics.[1, 2] Radak was not only a distinguished grammarian or a gifted biblical commentator, but functioned as a living bridge between the tradition of the "Golden Age" of Muslim Spain and the Jewish communities of Christian Europe, which at that time were beginning to shape their cultural and intellectual identity independently.[3, 4] His work extends over three principal planes that complement one another to form a holistic picture of a Jewish scholar in the Middle Ages: the study of language and the transformation of grammar into a systematic and accessible tool; the interpretation of Scripture according to peshat, combining philological depth with philosophical inquiry; and the polemical defense of the principles of Judaism in the face of Christianity and in the face of internal storms within the world of Torah.[3, 5, 6]
The Historical Background and the Family Dynasty: The Lamp of Light from Narbonne
In order to understand the depth of Radak's influence, one must first examine the geopolitical circumstances that led to his family's migration from Spain. His father, Rabbi Yosef Kimchi (the Rikam), was a prominent grammarian and commentator in southern Spain, who was forced to flee because of the persecutions of the Almohad dynasty (Almohads) around the year 4910 (1150).[3] The Almohads, Muslim zealots who conquered southern Spain and North Africa, set before the Jewish and Christian communities a cruel choice: conversion to Islam, death or emigration.[3] This wave of emigration, in the course of which the family of Maimonides (Rambam) and the Ibn Tibbon family also uprooted themselves, led to the transfer of the intellectual center of gravity of the "wisdom of Spain" to the region of Provence in southern France, which became an area of fascinating cultural contact between Arabic-Jewish culture and the Christian West.[3, 7]
Radak was born in Narbonne in 1160, in an atmosphere of cultural transformation. His father, Rabbi Yosef, brought with him the linguistic traditions of Rabbi Yehuda Chayyuj and Rabbi Yonah ibn Janach, who wrote in Judeo-Arabic, and began to translate and adapt them into Hebrew for the Jews of Europe who did not know the Arabic language.[1, 4] His father's early death, when David was only about ten years old, left his education in the hands of his elder brother, Rabbi Moshe Kimchi, who was himself an innovative and pioneering grammarian and commentator.[2, 3, 4] Rabbi Moshe's influence on Radak was decisive; David learned from him the foundations of grammar and exegesis, and many of the innovations later attributed to Radak in fact originate in the teaching of his brother, which he refined, expanded and disseminated to the masses.[2, 6]
The saying "If there is no flour (kemach), there is no Torah," which was coined for the members of the Kimchi family (an allusion to their name), faithfully expresses the view of their contemporaries: without the linguistic and methodological tools that the Kimchis provided, the understanding of the Torah remains deficient.[2, 3] In his youth Radak worked as a teacher for his livelihood, as his father had done, and this experience in teaching is clearly evident in his clear, didactic and organized style of writing, aimed at making complex knowledge accessible to a broad public.[3]
The Linguistic Revolution: Sefer ha-Mikhlol and Sefer ha-Shorashim
Radak's most famous contribution lies in the field of Hebrew linguistics. He is regarded as "the head of the grammarians" in the period of the Rishonim, and his books became a supreme authority for hundreds of years, both in the Jewish world and in the Christian world.[3, 4] Radak's central achievement was not necessarily the creation of entirely new theories, but his exceptional capacity for synthesis and organization. In the introduction to his book he describes himself as "a gleaner of ears of grain after the reaper," the reapers being the great Spanish grammarians who preceded him, chief among them Chayyuj and Ibn Janach.[4]
The Structure of the Grammatical Work
Radak's great work was originally a single comprehensive work intended to encompass all the rules of the Hebrew language and its lexicon, on a pattern similar to that of Rabbi Yonah ibn Janach.[4] Over the years, the printers divided the work into two separate books, each of which gained an eternal life of its own:
Sefer ha-Mikhlol (the grammatical part): this part deals with morphology and syntax. In it Radak analyzed the verbs, the nouns, the prepositions and the rules of inflection with almost mathematical precision.[4, 8] He definitively implanted the method of the triliteral root in the European sphere, and made it the basic working tool of every learner of Hebrew.
Sefer ha-Shorashim (the lexical part): this is a biblical dictionary arranged by the roots of the words. Radak not only defined the meaning of the words, but analyzed them in their biblical context, making extensive use of linguistic comparisons with Aramaic, Arabic, the language of the Sages and at times even the local language (Provençal).[4, 5]
Central Grammatical Innovations
One of Radak's greatest innovations, based on the teaching of his father and his brother, is the precise division of the vowels into five long vowels and five short vowels.[6] This division became an enduring asset in the teaching of Hebrew and is the basis of the entire system of vocalization accepted to this day. In addition, Radak contributed greatly to the understanding of the verbal system:
Defining the nif'al conjugation: it was Radak who established the recognition of the "nif'al" conjugation as the passive of the "kal" conjugation.[6]
Identifying the dagesh kal (Dagesh Lene): he set out the details of pronunciation and the rules of the letters bgd kpt (begadkefat) at the beginning of a word and after a quiescent sheva.[6]
The doctrine of the accents and the Masorah: in his book "Et Sofer" (The Scribe's Pen), Radak provided a comprehensive guide for scribes of Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot (STaM) concerning the rules for writing Torah scrolls, including the details of the Masorah Ketannah and Masorah Gedolah, the accents and the precise vocalization.[3, 6, 9]
The influence of the "Mikhlol" extended far beyond the Jewish world. In the Renaissance, when Christian scholars began to show interest in the original language of the Hebrew Bible, it was Radak's books that served them as a guide. Johannes Reuchlin, one of the fathers of Christian Hebraism, relied heavily on the "Mikhlol" and on "Sefer ha-Shorashim" in writing his grammar books, and thereby Radak became the father of the study of the Hebrew language in the eyes of the European academy as well.[3, 9, 10]
Biblical Exegesis: Peshat as a Rationalist Tool
After he had completed his monumental grammatical work, Radak turned to his second life's enterprise: the interpretation of Scripture. His commentaries cover extensive parts of the Hebrew Bible: the Book of Genesis, the Former and Latter Prophets, the Book of Psalms and Chronicles.[2, 11] His exegetical style is characterized by clarity, thoroughness and the combination of meticulous philological analysis with philosophical-rationalist insights deeply influenced by Maimonides (Rambam) and Ibn Ezra.[5, 6, 12]
The Methodology of the Commentary
Radak is counted among the great commentators of peshat, but his "peshat" is not merely a literal translation, but an in-depth analysis of the structure of the text. He devotes much attention to matters of the Masorah, keri and ketiv (the read and the written forms), and variant readings, noting at times that different versions of the Bible lay before him.[6, 8] In his commentaries on the Prophets, he deals with establishing the time of the prophets and describing the historical background of their prophecies, which gives the text a realistic-historical dimension.[2]
Unlike Rashi, who frequently incorporates aggadic midrashim into his commentary in order to answer linguistic or conceptual difficulties, Radak uses midrash only when it helps the understanding of the peshat or when he wishes to emphasize a particular moral message. He is greatly influenced by Abraham ibn Ezra in his tendency to be precise about language, but unlike Ibn Ezra, whose commentaries are at times enigmatic and brief ("a secret"), Radak expands his explanations and makes the commentary accessible and didactic.[4, 13, 14]
His Commentary on Psalms and Chronicles
Radak's commentary on the Book of Psalms is one of the most important and widespread works on this book. Apart from the linguistic treatment, Radak uses the Book of Psalms as a platform for discussing questions of providence, prayer and redemption.[2, 15] In his commentary on Chronicles, he succeeds in reconciling contradictions between the historical descriptions appearing in that book and those appearing in the books of Kings and Samuel, using the tools of textual comparison and linguistic precision.[2, 11]
His Philosophical and Esoteric Teaching
Radak was an ardent follower of Maimonides (Rambam) and of the rationalist approach. This influence is especially evident in his commentary on the Book of Genesis, where he seeks the moral and philosophical benefit in the stories of the Torah.[11, 12] In his view, the stories of the Torah were not given only in their plain sense; their reason is hidden, and they were meant to convey deep philosophical messages concerning the nature of the world and the soul.[12]
"Ma'aseh Bereshit" and "Ma'aseh Merkavah"
In accordance with the method of Maimonides, Radak identifies the Talmudic concepts "Ma'aseh Bereshit" (the Work of Creation) and "Ma'aseh Merkavah" (the Work of the Chariot) with the natural sciences (physics) and with metaphysics, respectively.[16, 17] He wrote detailed commentaries according to the esoteric way (nistar) on the passages of the Garden of Eden, Cain and Abel, and on chapter 1 of the Book of Ezekiel (Ma'aseh Merkavah).[6, 11, 12]
In his commentary on Ma'aseh Merkavah, Radak attempts to illuminate Ezekiel's prophetic vision as a representation of intellectual and cosmic forces. He sees in the "Chariot" the divine will that moves reality, while man, through his intellect and his will, can himself become "a chariot for the Divine Presence".[17] Nevertheless, Radak is careful in his language and emphasizes that the study of philosophy and engagement with the esoteric are fitting only for one whose "intellect is upright," whose fear of Heaven precedes his wisdom, and after he has established his knowledge of Torah and halakha.[4, 5]
The Doctrine of Prophecy and Providence
Radak adopted the view of Maimonides (Rambam) concerning the preconditions for prophecy (intellectual, moral and imaginative perfection), but he went further and noted that there is a theoretical possibility of prophecy also among the righteous of the nations of the world.[6] Regarding providence, he held that individual providence depends on the level of a person's intellectual cleaving to the Creator, but he presented an independent and interesting position according to which animals too may be subject to individual providence insofar as their action affects the fate of a human being.[6]
Radak in the Heat of Controversy: The Defense of Maimonides
In his last years, Radak was caught up in one of the greatest storms in the history of Judaism: "the Maimonidean controversy." The dispute, which broke out in the 13th century, concerned the philosophical path of Maimonides, and especially his books "Guide of the Perplexed" and "Sefer ha-Madda" (Book of Knowledge).[7, 18] The conservatives of northern France and Provence, headed by Rabbi Shlomo min ha-Har, saw the rationalist approach as a threat to simple faith and to the tradition of the Sages, and imposed a ban on the study of philosophy and on the books of Maimonides.[7, 18, 19]
Radak, despite his advanced age, took his stand without hesitation on the side of Maimonides' supporters. He saw in Maimonides the great luminary who had saved Jewish faith by providing an intellectual answer to the challenges of the period.[2, 4] Radak's involvement in the controversy was active and dramatic:
Public letters: Radak wrote sharp letters to Rabbi Shlomo min ha-Har and his disciples (such as Rabbi Yonah Gerondi), in which he defended the honor of Maimonides and attacked the extremism expressed in the appeal to the Christian Church to burn the Jewish books.[18, 19] He described this act as a terrible desecration of God's name and a betrayal within the people.
The journey to Spain (1232): at about the age of 72, Radak set out on a grueling journey from Provence to Spain in order to enlist the support of the communities of Castile and Aragon for the Maimonidean camp.[3, 6] He hoped to persuade Rabbi Yehuda Alfakhar of Toledo, a figure of immense influence, to join the defense of Maimonides.[6]
The confrontation with Alfakhar: the journey did not achieve its immediate aim. Alfakhar refused to support rationalism and sent Radak cutting letters of reply in which he accused the philosophers of undermining the foundations of miracle and prophecy.[6, 19] Radak fell ill during the journey and was forced to return to Narbonne, where he died a short time later.[3]
The Polemic with Christianity and the Influence on Gentile Scholars
Beyond the internal Jewish disputes, Radak worked in a Christian environment that was becoming more and more hostile. The 13th century was a period of the awakening of the Christian mission and of attempts by the Church to prove the truth of Christianity from the Jewish Bible. Radak saw it as his duty to respond to these attacks and to defend the original Jewish interpretation.[3, 9]
"Answers to the Christians" and the Commentary on Psalms
Radak's commentary on the Book of Psalms includes whole units of polemical material, sometimes called "Answers to the Christians" or "Radak's Disputation with the Christians".[11, 15] Radak attacks the Christian attempts to see in certain psalms (such as Psalms 2, 22 or 110) allusions to Jesus or to the principles of the Christian faith. He uses his scholarly tools to show that the Christian interpretation is based on textual corruptions, a lack of grammatical understanding or taking words out of their historical context.[6, 9]
For example, regarding Psalm 22, Radak rejects the Christological interpretation and emphasizes the suffering of the people of Israel in exile as the central theme of the psalm.[6] He comes out against the Christian claim that they are "the true Israel" (Verus Israel), and emphasizes the moral and religious superiority of Judaism and the eternal election of the people of Israel as "a nation of sages".[6]
Radak and Christian Hebraism
One of the fascinating phenomena in the reception of Radak is his enormous popularity among Christian scholars in later periods. In the period of the Reformation, when the Protestants sought to return to the "original text" (Ad Fontes), they found in Radak the most reliable guide. His influence on the King James Version of the Bible in English in 1611 was decisive, and scholars point out that many expressions and syntactic structures in this translation are based directly on Radak's commentaries and grammar.[9, 10]
Scholars such as Martin Luther and John Calvin valued him highly, and saw in him "the most faithful of the rabbis" (Fidelissimus inter Rabbinos).[10] His books "Mikhlol" and "Sefer ha-Shorashim" served as the basis for Christian dictionaries and grammar books, and thereby Radak contributed indirectly to a better understanding of Judaism and of the holy tongue in the Western world.[3, 10]
His Legacy for the Generations: "If There Is No Kimchi, There Is No Torah"
Radak's death in 1235 did not end his influence, but marked the beginning of his becoming a Jewish classic. His commentaries on the Prophets became an inseparable part of the "Mikraot Gedolot" editions, an achievement reserved for a select few, and they are studied to this day in every yeshiva and in every faculty of Bible.[2, 11]
A Comparison between Radak and the Principal Commentators of Peshat
In order to understand Radak's unique place within the world of exegesis, his method can be compared with that of Rashi and of Ibn Ezra:
Radak's work can be summed up as a successful and splendid attempt to create harmony among all the parts of Jewish knowledge. He succeeded in connecting worlds that at times seemed opposed: the Spanish tradition and Provençal scholarship; dry linguistic research and philosophical flight; and absolute faithfulness to tradition and openness to courageous rational inquiry.[4, 6, 7]
Rabbi David Kimchi was not merely "a gleaner of ears of grain," but the architect who designed the linguistic and exegetical infrastructure on which the Jewish bookshelf stands. His way, which combines scholarly depth with fear of Heaven and practical wisdom, has remained a model to be emulated by generations of researchers, rabbis and students of Hebrew and of the Bible. The exclamation of the author of Sefer Yuchasin, "If there is no Kimchi, there is no Torah," is not merely family praise, but a description of historical reality: without the work of Radak, our approach to the language of Scripture and to its spirit would have been significantly poorer and more deficient.[2, 3]
